storyline.arc: It started as an embedded terminal that wrapped Claude and OpenCode so the chat that produced a commit got committed too. Now it sandboxes worktrees, runs as a daemon, ships an MSI, reconstructs history you never tracked, and shows you a dashboard of how you actually spend your tokens.

eras.blurb: Worktrees got locked down with bubblewrap, shared sessions started asking twice before leaking secrets, sub-agent tokens finally got counted, and the whole thing was renamed aGiTrack.

eras.blurb: Background polling learned to back off when idle, git moved to its own thread, and after a POSIX-gated detour the reactor and an MSI pipeline landed on Windows.
eras.title: It stops burning CPU, and it runs on Windows

eras.blurb: Agent commits to the base repo got blocked, files started syncing both ways with the worktree, and a watermark that survives restarts made background mode cover commits the agent made on its own.
eras.title: Background mode and the persistent watermark

eras.blurb: It learned to reconstruct coding history it never watched, cache the expensive parts, and turn your token spend into personalized advice.
eras.title: Backtrace, efficiency insights, and a coach

eras.blurb: The dashboard and learn page shipped as static exports with a demo that politely refuses, concurrent writes stopped crashing, and the tool gained the ability to update itself.

moments.detail: The whole thing started from a simple itch: you talk to an agent for an hour, it edits fifteen files, and afterwards nobody can tell which prompt caused which change. So aGiT sits between you and the agent, reads the session log, and writes the commit for you. The first day's shape shifted fast: an early UI got thrown out for a tmux-like embedded terminal that same afternoon, and by midnight the Claude-only plumbing was torn open into a backend abstraction so opencode could ride the same rails.

The fix landed as a commit signed <aGiTrack>, written by the thing being fixed, which is either elegant or unsettling depending on your mood. Right after, someone pointed out that restarting agit kept only the last session name, and the tool went and fixed its own memory too.

moments.detail: The rename landed at 4am and the day turned into branch day: the ask was concurrent sessions on independent branches without touching the base branch in the repo directory, which meant the merge target had to become per-session rather than one global setting, and git-base-branch quietly stopped making sense.
moments.summary: Branch pickers, a merge-aware switch dialog, and a rule that agents may not auto-commit.

thoughts.note: The moment merge targets stopped being a repo-wide setting and became a property of each session.
thoughts.quote: I'd like to allow concurrent sessions on independent branches, without having to change the base branch in the repo directory. The user can select whether to apply merge changes to the base branch (default option) or to a different branch. When merging into a different branch than the one the repo's main directory is checked out, the status bar should emphasize that the branch the changes will be merged into is not the one on the directory. The emphasis may change if the user changes the branch on the repo directory.

thoughts.note: Working out that a finished session isn't safe to re-point until its changes are actually merged back, unless it was cancelled.
thoughts.quote: The branch switching dialog after a running session finishes should happen after the changes are merged into the original branch, not before. If a session is cancelled, the user can feel free to switch branches for that session.

moments.detail: The privacy warning that asks you to press Enter worked fine the first time, and then quietly stopped waiting on every restart after that. Turned out VS Code hands a reused terminal whatever keystrokes were sitting in its buffer, so the prompt read the leftovers and considered itself answered before you'd touched anything. The fix in runner.py was to drain the queued input first and only then ask the question, which is the kind of thing you only find because someone kept quitting the extension and starting it again.
moments.summary: The second extension start ignored keypresses until they drained the terminal's queued input.

thoughts.note: Two bugs reported in one breath, and the SSH theory for the startup error had just been ruled out.

The enter confirming to the warning is always required when aGiTrack starts. It seems there are multiple commands being sent to the terminal, one that changes the venv includes an enter and that "pressed" the enter for me.

thoughts.note: The clue was that it only ever happened on the second start, which pointed at leftover state rather than the prompt itself.

moments.detail: The whole thing started from a battery complaint: nobody wants a tracker spinning up file checks while the terminal sits untouched, so runner.py learned to notice that nobody had typed and no session was live, and back off. moments.summary: Idle backoff arrived, then a status-bar fix that flatly didn't work, then settings quietly vanishing on restart.

thoughts.note: Reading the constant they'd just added and deciding a fifth of a second is not a poll interval, it's a nervous tic.
thoughts.quote: ACTIVE_POLL_SECONDS (0.2s) sounds like a very small interval. No poll should be less than a second. Make sure that any file and folder checks are efficient too, instead of brute-forcelly checking though every file and folder. Only read parts of files and folders as needed. Use some list files function with last modified time if appropriate.

moments.detail: The worktree mode had a hole in it: an agent running loose in the base repo could just commit there, and aGiTrack's whole premise is that it owns those commits. So they wired a pre-commit guard into git/hooks.py, gated on an env variable so aGiTrack's own commits still pass, with a flag to turn it off for anyone who wants it off. Then came the honest test, "try to commit something to the base repo now and see if you get properly blocked", and the commit went through anyway.
moments.summary: Windows got a real installer and self-update; then a test commit to the base repo sailed straight through.

thoughts.note: Working out whether a git hook could tell an aGiTrack commit from a stray agent commit, and landing on an env variable as the signal.
thoughts.quote: Can we then disallow commits by agents to the base repo in the worktree mode using a similar hook? If it's possible to distinguish whether to apply the hook or not using an env variable, then it should be fine. The goal: agents running inside aGiTrack without the no-worktree option should not be allowed to commit into the base repo directly; the user and agents running outside aGiTrack shouldn't be affected by this restriction at all and they can commit freely.

thoughts.note: Testing the guard by trying to break it, and noticing the error message was handing the agent an escape hatch.

moments.detail: The first ask was blunt: copy everything from the base repo into the worktree, and stop deleting the worktree on exit. What followed was a day of the same person saying "still doesn't work" while resuming with --no-worktree kept opening an older session, and .claude/ kept getting offered up for staging as if it were real work. By the end they'd flipped the base-to-worktree prompt to default Yes, told it to check dotfiles and underscore files too, and taught the copy-back to shut up about files that were already byte-identical.
moments.summary: A fresh worktree lacked the environment to actually work in, so they copied the base repo across.

thoughts.note: Realising a worktree without the base repo's untracked environment is just an empty room you can't build in.
thoughts.quote: On worktree creation, copy all the files from the base repo to the worktree directory, so that the full environment is available in the worktree directory as in the base repo. Separately, sessions running previously in a worktree should be resumable from the base repo once the user turns on --no-worktree option. The same should be resumable if the user renames the session and thus causing the worktree to have a different directory.

thoughts.note: After watching no-worktree mode keep editing inside the worktree anyway, they concluded the safest thing was to offer to delete it outright.
thoughts.quote: What is your working directory now?

moments.detail: The whole thing started with someone SSH'd into a remote box, running `agitrack -d`, and getting a dashboard bound to localhost that nobody could reach. The fix in agitrack/metrics/web.py binds all interfaces and prints the ssh -L line you can paste straight into a second terminal, which is the kind of help you only write after typing it by hand a few dozen times. Later the same day, cleaning up the landing page, the git blame box got deleted for a plainer reason: most people don't know what git blame is, and nine boxes make a tidy grid on a laptop.
moments.summary: Remote users couldn't reach the dashboard, so it now prints a paste-ready tunnel command; git blame box got cut too.

thoughts.note: Realising the dashboard was fine locally and useless everywhere else, and that a firewall-permitting bind plus a tunnel hint covers both cases.
thoughts.quote: When running agitrack -d or agitrack --backtrace in a remote terminal, the webpage should be binded to all network interfaces (0.0.0.0), so that someone can open it with the remote's IP and port if firewall rules allow. If firewall does not allow it, the command line message to the user should say exactly what needs to be done for ssh forwarding, so that the user can copy-paste the commands without having to understand it further. Also, make the ports for new web backends allocated continuously for multiple instances; currently starting from the second instance it is quite random.

thoughts.note: Cutting a box for a vocabulary reason, and noticing at the same time that 'nothing leaves your machine' isn't true once a remote git repo is involved.
thoughts.quote: Many people don't know what git blame is. Remove that box please. It's also good to keep the boxes to 9 since that will be a grid when shown on laptop browser. Don't say "Nothing leaves your machine", remote git repos are also not on your machine. Probably say something like "Nothing externally tracked"

moments.detail: The demo pages went missing right after a release, and the request had the tone of someone refreshing a live site: fix it immediately. The workflow had been pointed at the wrong build source, so the deploy shipped everything except the static demos. Later that day the ask shifted from breakage to patience: the backtrace dashboard should pick up new sessions on its own, but the prompt was explicit that watching for changes must not burn compute, so the change in agitrack/metrics/backtrace.py leans on cheap change detection rather than re-reading the world.

moments.detail: The first version came out chronological, with a "raw material" dump under each story, and reading it top-down meant wading through months to reach yesterday. So they flipped it: latest first, commits attached to each story with a toggle for file changes, and no raw material section at all. The zoom rework came later and was blunter, because an act was cheerfully announcing Windows had landed when Windows integration had been in for a month, and each part was quietly starting from the newest end instead of covering its actual date range.
moments.summary: Raw material section cut, chapters trimmed to the latest few, timeline rezoomed to span real date ranges.

thoughts.note: They wanted the page to read like news, not an archive, and noticed the chain of thought was getting truncated mid-word.
thoughts.quote: The story line should start with the latest first. Remove the raw material section; the commits are only linked to each story. In each story's commits, it should first show the commit message and have a button to toggle to show file changes. Make each story much shorter too.
